1	Timing of Anterior Cruciate
2	Ligament Surgery
3	Bálint Zsidai, MDa,*, Janina Kaarre, MD, MSca,b,
4	Eric Narup, MD, MSca, Kristian Samuelsson, MD, PhD, MSca,c
5	
6	
7	 KEYWORDS
8	  Anterior cruciate ligament  ACL  Reconstruction  Timing  Knee ligament surgery
9	  Knee injuries  Arthroscopy  Sports medicine
10	
11	
12	 KEY POINTS
13	  There is considerable uncertainty surrounding the definition of early and delayed anterior
14	   cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), with the definition for early surgery ranging from
15	   days to months and for delayed surgery ranging from weeks to years in the current
16	   literature.
17	  Modern arthroscopic surgical techniques and early rehabilitation have mitigated the risk of
18	   arthrofibrosis and postoperative stiffness with early ACLR.
19	  Early ACLR is shown to be equivalent or superior to delayed ACLR in terms of clinical out-
20	   comes, subjective postoperative knee function, the incidence of intra-articular injury
21	   within the timeframe between injury and surgery, as well as cost-effectiveness.
22	  Concomitant surgical procedures addressing anterolateral instability, anteromedial insta-
23	   bility, and meniscus injury may be more advantageous when performed in conjunction
24	   with early ACLR.
25	
26	
27	
28	
29	INTRODUCTION
30	
31	Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears are one of the most frequent injuries to the liga-
32	mentous structures of the knee. Although arthroscopic ACL reconstruction (ACLR) is
33	the gold standard for the surgical treatment of ACL tears, the ACL surgeon needs to
34	be aware of the wide range of patient-related, injury-related, and surgery-related factors
35	influencing treatment outcomes. Although the timing of ACLR is one such factor,
36	there currently is no clear consensus about the definition of early and delayed ACLR
37	or the optimal timing of surgery following ACL tears. Surgical treatment is generally
38	
39	
40	 a
41	   Department of Orthopaedics, Institute of Clinical Sciences, Sahlgrenska Academy, University
42	 of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden; b Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, UPMC Freddie Fu
43	 Sports Medicine Center, University of Pittsburgh, 3200 South Water Street, Pittsburgh, PA, USA;
44	 c
45	   Department of Orthopaedics, Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Göteborgsvägen 31, 431 30
46	 Mölndal, Sweden
47	 * Corresponding author. Göteborgsvägen 31, Mölndal 431 80, Sweden.
48	 E-mail address: balint.zsidai@gu.se
49	
50	 Clin Sports Med - (2023) -–-
51	 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csm.2023.08.002                                          sportsmed.theclinics.com
52	 0278-5919/23/ª 2023 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
53	
54	
55	  Downloaded for Anonymous User (n/a) at The Ohio State University from ClinicalKey.com by Elsevier on January 02,
56	   2024. For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2024. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
57	 2     Zsidai et al
58	
59	
60	
61	      recommended to restore knee stability in patients with high demand for knee-strenuous
62	      activity but the decision of when to perform ACLR varies among surgeons and may be
63	      influenced by factors such as patient age, activity level, and associated injuries.
64	         Acute knee ligament injuries were historically treated with open repair followed by
65	      postoperative immobilization with a cast. Because early surgery often resulted in a
66	      high incidence of knee stiffness and arthrofibrosis, delayed surgical treatment was
67	      proposed as an alternative, which provides time for joint inflammation to subside, re-
68	      covery in knee range of motion (ROM), and restoration of muscle strength, potentially
69	      diminishing the rate of postoperative joint stiffness. However, a greater incidence of
70	      secondary intra-articular damage and potential quadriceps atrophy were proposed
71	      as drawbacks inherent to delayed ACL surgery. As a result, the complex interplay
72	      between the risk of timing-associated complications, economic factors, surgeon pref-
73	      erence, and patient motivation to return to preinjury activity level ultimately determines
74	      surgical timing in ACLR.
75	         Despite the growing awareness of the role of surgical timing, consensus surround-
76	      ing the definition of the cutoff time interval from injury distinguishing early and delayed
77	      ACLR is currently lacking. Cutoff time intervals ranging between 8 days and1
78	      12 months2 have been reported for early isolated ACLR, whereas a cutoff as early
79	      as 3 weeks was used for delayed isolated ACLR in a recent meta-analysis,3 empha-
80	      sizing the heterogeneity with respect to timing among existing studies.
81	         The setting of multiligament knee injury (MLKI) may also influence the decision of the
82	      operating surgeon to opt for early or delayed ACLR. Although several studies investi-
83	      gated outcomes following ACLR combined with the surgical or nonsurgical treatment
84	      of concomitant knee ligament injuries, evidence is currently inconclusive regarding the
85	      optimal timing of surgical treatment of MLKIs where ACLR is performed.4
86	         The aim of this review is to critically assess the current literature regarding the
87	      impact of surgical timing in the setting of ACL injury treatment on a broad range of
88	      postoperative outcomes. A thorough analysis of the inconsistencies surrounding the
89	      definition of early and delayed ACLR, the influence of early versus delayed surgery
90	      on the prevalence of associated knee injuries and the influence of surgical timing on
91	      functional and clinical patient outcomes may facilitate evidence-based decision-mak-
92	      ing for surgeons performing isolated ACLR and ACLR in the setting of MLKI (Fig. 1).
93	
94	
95	      A RATIONALE FOR THE NEED OF CLEARER DEFINITIONS OF EARLY AND DELAYED
96	      ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION
97	
98	      During the recent years, several systematic reviews and meta-analyses attempted to
99	      clarify the association between ACLR timing relative to the incidence of ACL injury and
100	      postoperative outcomes.3,5–10 Although most of these studies did not determine clear
101	      differences in outcomes related to early or delayed surgery, there is unanimous agree-
102	      ment that conclusions are hampered by the heterogeneity of existing studies concern-
103	      ing the definition of early and delayed surgical timing. One systematic review
104	      considering the definitions of acute and chronic orthopedic conditions determined
105	      early ACL tears to be less than 6 week old with respect to the time of injury, whereas
106	      chronic ACL tears were defined as more than 6 month old relative to the time of injury.
107	      However, a large proportion of studies in the existing literature define ACLR as delayed
108	      even when performed before 6 weeks of ACL injury, which decreases the reliability of
109	      the currently available evidence.10,11 Furthermore, the role of the time interval between
110	      6 weeks and 6 months relative to the incidence of ACL injury remains unaddressed
111	      and the current definition of early and delayed ACLR remains arbitrary rather than
112	      explicit. Ain improved understanding of the inflammatory state of the knee joint in
113	
114	    Downloaded for Anonymous User (n/a) at The Ohio State University from ClinicalKey.com by Elsevier on January 02,
115	     2024. For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2024. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
116	                                                                                     Timing of ACL Surgery               3
117	
118	
119	
120	
121	Fig. 1. The potential advantages and disadvantages of early versus delayed ACLR. ACLR,
122	anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction; MLKI, multiple knee ligament injury.
123	
124	the setting of ACL injury was also proposed to help define early and delayed surgical
125	timing for ACLR. Synovial proinflammatory cytokine levels have been shown to in-
126	crease within 24 to 72 hours of ACL injury, followed by decreasing levels during a
127	1-month interval before surgery.12 However, the clinical utility of synovial biomarkers
128	in determining the timing of ACLR remains unclear.
129	   Despite the lack of clarity surrounding early and delayed ACLR, a recent study from
130	the Swedish National Knee Ligament Registry determined that patients with early
131	ACLR (<1 year from injury) reported a superior rate of acceptable knee-related symp-
132	tom state and improved overall knee function compared with patients initial nonoper-
133	ative treatment followed by delayed ACLR.13 However, the time from injury to surgery
134	was on average 6 months (standard deviation 5 2.4 months) in the early ACLR group
135	(n 5 20,352) with the appropriate threshold for early ACLR remaining inconclusive.13 In
136	a recent systematic review and meta-analysis, comparison of 5 randomized controlled
137	trials (RCTs) determined that patients with early isolated ACLR were on average
138	treated 44 days earlier compared with patients who underwent delayed ACLR, with
139	no difference in postoperative outcomes.10 This broad time interval makes it difficult
140	to define a clear cutoff for early and delayed ACLR and suggests that the context of
141	surgical timing should be considered on a spectrum of months rather than a few
142	weeks to show an impact on postoperative outcomes. Importantly, there is a lack of
143	RCTs assessing the role of ACLR timing in the context of surgically treated MLKIs.
144	One recent multicenter RCT reported that a complete tear of the ACL was involved
145	in 56.5% of MLKIs and that the average time from injury to primary multiligament
146	knee surgery was 64 days (interquartile range 5 29–190 days).4 Consequently, further
147	high-level studies are required to determine the impact of ACLR timing in the setting of
148	both surgically treated isolated ACL injuries and MLKIs.
149	
150	THE INCIDENCE OF POSTOPERATIVE STIFFNESS AND ARTHROFIBROSIS WITH
151	ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION TIMING
152	
153	Arthrofibrosis of the knee joint is caused by excessive scar tissue formation, resulting
154	in pain and limited potential for the patient to regain the terminal 5 of extension
155	
156	  Downloaded for Anonymous User (n/a) at The Ohio State University from ClinicalKey.com by Elsevier on January 02,
157	   2024. For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2024. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
158	 4     Zsidai et al
159	
160	
161	
162	      throughout knee ROM. The timing of ACL surgery has been reported to have a crucial
163	      effect on the risk of developing postoperative arthrofibrosis. A study performed in
164	      1991 found that open ACLR performed within a week of acute ACL injury resulted in
165	      an increased rate of postoperative stiffness compared with ACLR performed at least
166	      3 weeks from the time of acute ACL injury.14 In the same study, delayed surgery and
167	      accelerated rehabilitation (uncommon at the time) resulted in an earlier return of strength
168	      and a significantly lower incidence of arthrofibrosis. However, delayed ACLR has been
169	      associated with an increased risk of quadriceps atrophy, which may prolong postoper-
170	      ative rehabilitation and may negatively influence postoperative knee function.15
171	         With the advancement of arthroscopic knee surgery as the gold standard for the
172	      surgical treatment of ACL injury, the prevalence of arthrofibrosis and postoperative
173	      stiffness showed a diminishing tendency in patients undergoing ACLR, most likely
174	      due to early rehabilitation programs and improved surgical techniques.6 More recent
175	      studies failed to demonstrate increased rates of postoperative stiffness, arthrofibrosis,
176	      and ROM deficits with a variety of cutoff thresholds between early and delayed ACLR
177	      (<2 weeks, <3 weeks, <10 weeks and beyond).16 One RCT found that early (<8 days
178	      from injury to surgery) ACLR resulted in no ROM deficit at the 6-month or 24-month
179	      follow-up compared with delayed (6–10 weeks from injury to surgery) ACLR.1,17
180	      Additionally, early (<8 days from injury to surgery) surgery resulted in superior isoki-
181	      netic knee flexion strength at the 24-month follow-up compared with delayed (6–
182	      10 weeks from injury to surgery) treatment.17 Furthermore, a case series of early
183	      patellar tendon ACLRs (n 5 25) performed 9 days or lesser from injury to surgery
184	      did not identify any patients with a postoperative knee extension deficit greater than
185	      3 and knee flexion deficit greater than 5 compared with the contralateral knee at
186	      the final follow-up.18 Authors of the referenced studies highlight the prominent role
187	      of modern arthroscopic techniques and accelerated rehabilitation protocols to facili-
188	      tate early restoration of knee ROM during the postoperative period.17,18 In contrast,
189	      one recent retrospective study of 29,888 patients found that a 6 week or longer delay
190	      of ACLR reduces the 2-year likelihood of surgical treatment of arthrofibrosis by 65% in
191	      patients aged younger than 40 years.19 Although the timing of ACL surgery may affect
192	      the likelihood of postoperative arthrofibrosis, existing evidence suggests that early
193	      surgery combined with accelerated rehabilitation can lead to earlier return of strength
194	      and an infrequent incidence of arthrofibrosis. Conversely, delayed surgery may in-
195	      crease the risk of quadriceps atrophy and negatively influence postoperative knee
196	      function, especially problematic for high-level athletes who aim for rapid return to
197	      preinjury activity levels.
198	
199	
200	      COMPARISON OF CLINICAL OUTCOMES AFTER EARLY AND DELAYED ANTERIOR
201	      CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION
202	
203	      During the years, surgical timing was determined as an influential factor on clinical out-
204	      comes after ACLR. Several studies compared the effects of early and delayed ACLR
205	      on the risk of graft failure and revision surgery. Economic and decision analysis using
206	      registry-based patient data from the Knee Anterior Cruciate Ligament Nonsurgical
207	      versus Surgical Treatment trial and Multicenter Orthopedic Outcomes Network cohort
208	      determined that early isolated ACLR results in less sick-leave days (on average
209	        31.6 days) and superior gains in Quality Adjusted Life Years compared with rehabil-
210	      itation with optional delayed ACLR. However, findings are conflicting regarding the as-
211	      sociation between ACLR timing and the risk of revision ACLR. One study of 11,867
212	      patients reported an increased risk of revision ACLR with delayed ACLR (performed
213	      at least 6 months after injury) compared with early ACLR (performed within 2 months
214	
215	    Downloaded for Anonymous User (n/a) at The Ohio State University from ClinicalKey.com by Elsevier on January 02,
216	     2024. For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2024. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
217	                                                                                     Timing of ACL Surgery               5
218	
219	
220	
221	of injury).20 Conversely, an increased revision risk (relative risk 5 2.07) was reported in
222	patients undergoing early isolated ACLR (defined as surgery performed within
223	3 months of injury).21 Furthermore, a 2 to 3-fold revision ACLR rate was found in pa-
224	tients undergoing ACLR within 90 days of injury compared with patients undergoing
225	surgery after 365 days from injury.22 However, it is worth noting that the likelihood
226	of revision after early and delayed ACLR is likely influenced by factors such as activity
227	level after surgery and patient age, rather than the timing of surgery itself.23 Therefore,
228	the risk of revision should be considered multifactorial and should not solely rely on the
229	timing of surgery.
230	
231	COMPARISON OF FUNCTIONAL OUTCOMES AFTER EARLY AND DELAYED ANTERIOR
232	CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION
233	
234	Another major controversy in ACL surgery is whether early or delayed ACLR leads to
235	superior objective and subjective outcomes for patients. Several studies report com-
236	parable clinical and outcomes superior knee stability because of both early and
237	delayed ACLR.24,25 One systematic review found similar tibiofemoral laxity, assessed
238	with the KT-1000 arthrometer, Lachman test, and the pivot shift test, in patients who
239	underwent early ACLR (performed within 1 month of injury) versus those who under-
240	went delayed ACLR (performed >8 weeks after injury).26 No significant differences
241	in postoperative knee ROM were found between the 2 groups.26 Additionally, one
242	recent study showed comparable patient-reported outcomes, with significant im-
243	provements in all subscales of the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score
244	(KOOS) and favorable return rate to preinjury Tegner activity level after both early
245	and delayed ACLR.17 Notably, a high proportion of patients in both the early and
246	delayed ACLR groups were able to return to Tegner activity level 6 or higher, suggest-
247	ing surgical timing may have a limited influence on the rate of return to sport.17 Further-
248	more, objective International Knee Documentation Committee scores were shown to
249	be similar among patient groups, with the majority of (82% vs 71%, respectively) of
250	patients having grade AB pivot shift at the 12-month postoperative follow-up, indica-
251	tive of restored knee laxity because of both early and delayed ACLR.17
252	   Further research showed that patients with early, hamstring tendon ACLR achieve
253	superior outcomes in terms of postoperative isokinetic knee flexion strength after
254	2 years compared with patients who underwent delayed ACLR.27 Specifically, patients
255	with early surgery achieved significantly greater improvement in flexor strength at 180
256	(8.1% improvement) and 240 (9.4% improvement) per second, without significant
257	improvement in extensor strength.27 In the same study, early ACLR was associated
258	with fewer sick-leave days and decreased socioeconomic costs compared with
259	delayed ACLR.27 Consequently, while both early and delayed surgery seem to yield
260	good to excellent functional outcomes, a combination of functional outcomes should
261	be assessed to determine the optimal timing of isolated ACLR.
262	
263	The Impact of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Timing on the Incidence
264	of Secondary Intra-articular Injury
265	Due to conflicting results in the current literature, the influence of ACLR timing on the
266	incidence of secondary intra-articular injury remains a topic of debate. Delayed sur-
267	gery was proposed to lead to meniscal8 and chondral7 damage secondary to knee
268	instability because of prolonged ACL deficiency.28
269	  One retrospective study of 226 patients who underwent primary ACLR found that sur-
270	gery delayed beyond 7 months of injury was associated with 4.1-fold odds of the pres-
271	ence of medial meniscus injury recoded at surgery compared with ACLR performed
272	
273	  Downloaded for Anonymous User (n/a) at The Ohio State University from ClinicalKey.com by Elsevier on January 02,
274	   2024. For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2024. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
275	 6     Zsidai et al
276	
277	
278	
279	      within 6 months of injury.29 Furthermore, patients with primary ACLR beyond 5 months
280	      from injury had 1.9-fold odds for lateral meniscus injury compared with surgery per-
281	      formed within 4 months of injury.29 A systematic review performed in 2018 found that
282	      6 of the 7 included studies implicated the role of prolonged knee instability with delayed
283	      primary ACLR in the development of medial meniscus injury (odds ratio [OR] range
284	      3.46–11.56), despite an inconclusive association of prolonged instability with lateral
285	      meniscus injury rate.30 The more predominant role of chronic ACL deficiency on the
286	      prevalence of subsequent medial meniscus injury is further supported by additional
287	      recent studies from the literature, which also highlight inferior rates of repairability of
288	      these lesions with time.23,31–34 A recent systematic review and meta-analysis
289	      concluded that primary ACLR delayed beyond 3 months of ACL injury results in a
290	      2.24-fold odds of medical meniscus injury compared with surgery performed earlier
291	      than 3 months, whereas the causal effect of timing on the prevalence of meniscal in-
292	      juries remains unclear.8 Consequently, early ACLR may be recommended to protect
293	      the integrity of the medial meniscus from prolonged knee instability.
294	         During the last 20 years, several studies corroborated the negative influence of
295	      delayed ACL surgery on chondral wear.2,35,36 One systematic review of 40 articles found
296	      a positive correlation between the rate of cartilage injury and ACLR delayed beyond
297	      12 months (risk ratio 5 0.42).31 Furthermore, retrospective analysis of 3976 patients
298	      undergoing isolated primary ACLR at a single institution determined that surgery per-
299	      formed 12 months from injury resulted in a 1.20 OR of cartilage injury rate.32 Additionally,
300	      one United States integrated health-care registry study found that 24.8% of patients
301	      with early (<3 weeks from injury to surgery) ACLR presented with cartilage injury at
302	      the time of surgery, whereas patients with delayed (9 months) ACLR had a 40.0%
303	      rate of concurrent cartilage injury.23 One recent systematic review and meta-analysis
304	      compared cartilage injury rates as a function of 3-month, 6-month, and 12-month
305	      time intervals from ACL injury to ACLR with ACLR performed within 3 months of injury.7
306	      The analysis of 14 studies included in the final synthesis found an increase of the prev-
307	      alence of chondral injury at each time interval compared with early surgery (<3 months),
308	      with low-grade cartilage injuries becoming prevalent after the 3-month interval
309	      (OR 5 1.91) and high-grade cartilage injuries becoming more prominent after 12 months
310	      (OR 5 3.06).7 In contrast, another recent meta-analysis found no difference in the rate of
311	      cartilage injury between early (<3 weeks) and delayed (>6 weeks) ACLR is prevalent in
312	      the setting of MLKI but not in isolated ligamentous injury only involving the ACL.10 How-
313	      ever, heterogeneity between different syntheses performed on the available literature is
314	      likely due to different interpretations of cutoff values for early and delayed surgery.
315	      Despite the difficulty to determine the causality between surgical timing and the devel-
316	      opment of intra-articular injuries due to the inability to obtain baseline MRIs at the time of
317	      injury, current evidence predominantly suggests that early ACLR has a protective effect
318	      on the development of further intra-articular pathology with time. Prevention of chondral
319	      damage in patients with ACL injury is essential because patients with concomitant
320	      partial-thickness and full-thickness cartilage lesions at the time of ACLR report inferior
321	      5-year subjective knee function measured with the KOOS.37
322	
323	
324	      INTERPLAY BETWEEN ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION TIMING
325	      AND CONCURRENT SURGICAL INTERVENTIONS
326	
327	      Injury to the ACL is frequently accompanied by concomitant injuries and adequate
328	      treatment consists of addressing concurrent pathologic condition with concurrent
329	      surgical interventions. However, the interplay between additional surgical interven-
330	      tions concurrent with ACLR and surgical timing remains to be clarified. Patients with
331	
332	    Downloaded for Anonymous User (n/a) at The Ohio State University from ClinicalKey.com by Elsevier on January 02,

336	
337	
338	high-grade rotatory knee instability may benefit from additional lateral extra-articular
339	interventions concurrent to ACLR to restore rotatory knee stability.38,39 One recent
340	study compared postoperative outcomes among a cohort of patients with early
341	(<8 weeks from injury to surgery) combined ACLR and anterolateral ligament (ALL)
342	reconstruction and a cohort with delayed (>8 weeks from injury to surgery) combined
343	ACLR and ALL reconstruction, with no differences in objective knee stability, subjec-
344	tive knee function, and graft failure rates (2.9% and 2.1%, respectively).40 Further-
345	more, patients with ACL injury often present with concomitant injury to the medial
346	collateral ligament (MCL).4,41 Although the choice between surgical or nonoperative
347	treatment of MCL injuries concomitant to ACLR remains a controversial topic, it was
348	recently reported that as few as 10% of patients nonoperatively treated for MCL injury
349	concurrent with ACLR return to preinjury activity level.42 Due to the detrimental effect
350	of persistent valgus laxity on the integrity of intra-articular soft-tissue, prolonged reha-
351	bilitation with incomplete healing and stress on the ACL graft, early combined ACLR
352	and MCL reconstruction is increasingly favored.43 Consequently, patients with antero-
353	lateral and anteromedial instability in the setting of surgically treated ACL injury may
354	benefit from early ACLR with concurrent lateral extra-articular tenodesis and MCL
355	reconstruction. Repair of treatable meniscus pathologic condition in conjunction
356	with ACLR is also considered advantageous in patients with ACL injury. It was reported
357	that 77.6% of meniscus injuries were repaired concomitant to early (<6 months from
358	injury to surgery) ACLR, whereas only 46.7% of meniscus injuries were repaired with
359	delayed (>6 months from injury to surgery) ACLR. Additionally, meniscus repair per-
360	formed in the setting of early (<48 hours from injury) ACLR resulted in lower rates of
361	extension deficit between 3 and 5 at the 12-month postoperative follow-up
362	compared with delayed (performed in the inflammation-free period) ACLR and
363	meniscus repair (3.7% vs 22.2%, respectively).11 Therefore, early surgical timing for
364	ACLR may be preferred in highly active patients with concurrent repairable meniscus
365	injury to prevent the incidence of downstream chondral wear and posttraumatic OA.
366	
367	SUMMARY
368	
369	In light of the current evidence, an improved understanding of surgical timing is war-
370	ranted to optimize patient outcomes with ACLR in the setting of isolated ACL and
371	MLKIs. Although interpretation of the existing data is hampered by inconsistent defi-
372	nitions of surgical timing, early ACLR performed within weeks of injury may result in
373	equivalent to superior clinical and functional outcomes. Importantly, early ACLR
374	seems to be beneficial for decreasing the incidence of medial meniscus and chondral
375	injury by avoiding prolonged knee instability, with excellent clinical and functional out-
376	comes and no marked increase in the risk of postoperative arthrofibrosis compared
377	with delayed surgery. Future studies are required to clarify the cutoff between early
378	and delayed surgeries to determine the influence of concurrent surgical procedures
379	on optimal surgical timing and to explore the role of surgical timing in the treatment
380	of patients with MLKIs.
381	
382	CLINICS CARE POINTS

386	  Delayed ACLR may increase the incidence of secondary intraarticular injuries and quadriceps
387	   atrophy, with a potentially negative impact on postoperative outcomes.
388	  Inconsistent definitions of early and delayed ACLR may lead to ambiguity and hinder
389	   evidence-based decision-making.

Timing of Anterior Cruciate
Ligament Surgery
Bálint Zsidai, MDa,*, Janina Kaarre, MD, MSca,b,
Eric Narup, MD, MSca, Kristian Samuelsson, MD, PhD, MSca,c


 KEYWORDS
  Anterior cruciate ligament  ACL  Reconstruction  Timing  Knee ligament surgery
  Knee injuries  Arthroscopy  Sports medicine


 KEY POINTS
  There is considerable uncertainty surrounding the definition of early and delayed anterior
   cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), with the definition for early surgery ranging from
   days to months and for delayed surgery ranging from weeks to years in the current
   literature.
  Modern arthroscopic surgical techniques and early rehabilitation have mitigated the risk of
   arthrofibrosis and postoperative stiffness with early ACLR.
  Early ACLR is shown to be equivalent or superior to delayed ACLR in terms of clinical out-
   comes, subjective postoperative knee function, the incidence of intra-articular injury
   within the timeframe between injury and surgery, as well as cost-effectiveness.
  Concomitant surgical procedures addressing anterolateral instability, anteromedial insta-
   bility, and meniscus injury may be more advantageous when performed in conjunction
   with early ACLR.




INTRODUCTION

Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears are one of the most frequent injuries to the liga-
mentous structures of the knee. Although arthroscopic ACL reconstruction (ACLR) is
the gold standard for the surgical treatment of ACL tears, the ACL surgeon needs to
be aware of the wide range of patient-related, injury-related, and surgery-related factors
influencing treatment outcomes. Although the timing of ACLR is one such factor,
there currently is no clear consensus about the definition of early and delayed ACLR
or the optimal timing of surgery following ACL tears. Surgical treatment is generally

 2     Zsidai et al



      recommended to restore knee stability in patients with high demand for knee-strenuous
      activity but the decision of when to perform ACLR varies among surgeons and may be
      influenced by factors such as patient age, activity level, and associated injuries.
         Acute knee ligament injuries were historically treated with open repair followed by
      postoperative immobilization with a cast. Because early surgery often resulted in a
      high incidence of knee stiffness and arthrofibrosis, delayed surgical treatment was
      proposed as an alternative, which provides time for joint inflammation to subside, re-
      covery in knee range of motion (ROM), and restoration of muscle strength, potentially
      diminishing the rate of postoperative joint stiffness. However, a greater incidence of
      secondary intra-articular damage and potential quadriceps atrophy were proposed
      as drawbacks inherent to delayed ACL surgery. As a result, the complex interplay
      between the risk of timing-associated complications, economic factors, surgeon pref-
      erence, and patient motivation to return to preinjury activity level ultimately determines
      surgical timing in ACLR.
         Despite the growing awareness of the role of surgical timing, consensus surround-
      ing the definition of the cutoff time interval from injury distinguishing early and delayed
      ACLR is currently lacking. Cutoff time intervals ranging between 8 days and1
      12 months2 have been reported for early isolated ACLR, whereas a cutoff as early
      as 3 weeks was used for delayed isolated ACLR in a recent meta-analysis,3 empha-
      sizing the heterogeneity with respect to timing among existing studies.
         The setting of multiligament knee injury (MLKI) may also influence the decision of the
      operating surgeon to opt for early or delayed ACLR. Although several studies investi-
      gated outcomes following ACLR combined with the surgical or nonsurgical treatment
      of concomitant knee ligament injuries, evidence is currently inconclusive regarding the
      optimal timing of surgical treatment of MLKIs where ACLR is performed.4
         The aim of this review is to critically assess the current literature regarding the
      impact of surgical timing in the setting of ACL injury treatment on a broad range of
      postoperative outcomes. A thorough analysis of the inconsistencies surrounding the
      definition of early and delayed ACLR, the influence of early versus delayed surgery
      on the prevalence of associated knee injuries and the influence of surgical timing on
      functional and clinical patient outcomes may facilitate evidence-based decision-mak-
      ing for surgeons performing isolated ACLR and ACLR in the setting of MLKI (Fig. 1).


      A RATIONALE FOR THE NEED OF CLEARER DEFINITIONS OF EARLY AND DELAYED
      ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION

      During the recent years, several systematic reviews and meta-analyses attempted to
      clarify the association between ACLR timing relative to the incidence of ACL injury and
      postoperative outcomes.3,5–10 Although most of these studies did not determine clear
      differences in outcomes related to early or delayed surgery, there is unanimous agree-
      ment that conclusions are hampered by the heterogeneity of existing studies concern-
      ing the definition of early and delayed surgical timing. One systematic review
      considering the definitions of acute and chronic orthopedic conditions determined
      early ACL tears to be less than 6 week old with respect to the time of injury, whereas
      chronic ACL tears were defined as more than 6 month old relative to the time of injury.
      However, a large proportion of studies in the existing literature define ACLR as delayed
      even when performed before 6 weeks of ACL injury, which decreases the reliability of
      the currently available evidence.10,11 Furthermore, the role of the time interval between
      6 weeks and 6 months relative to the incidence of ACL injury remains unaddressed
      and the current definition of early and delayed ACLR remains arbitrary rather than
      explicit. Ain improved understanding of the inflammatory state of the knee joint in

   Despite the lack of clarity surrounding early and delayed ACLR, a recent study from
the Swedish National Knee Ligament Registry determined that patients with early
ACLR (<1 year from injury) reported a superior rate of acceptable knee-related symp-
tom state and improved overall knee function compared with patients initial nonoper-

was on average 6 months (standard deviation 5 2.4 months) in the early ACLR group
(n 5 20,352) with the appropriate threshold for early ACLR remaining inconclusive.13 In
a recent systematic review and meta-analysis, comparison of 5 randomized controlled
trials (RCTs) determined that patients with early isolated ACLR were on average
treated 44 days earlier compared with patients who underwent delayed ACLR, with
no difference in postoperative outcomes.10 This broad time interval makes it difficult
to define a clear cutoff for early and delayed ACLR and suggests that the context of
surgical timing should be considered on a spectrum of months rather than a few
weeks to show an impact on postoperative outcomes. Importantly, there is a lack of
RCTs assessing the role of ACLR timing in the context of surgically treated MLKIs.
One recent multicenter RCT reported that a complete tear of the ACL was involved
in 56.5% of MLKIs and that the average time from injury to primary multiligament
knee surgery was 64 days (interquartile range 5 29–190 days).4 Consequently, further
high-level studies are required to determine the impact of ACLR timing in the setting of
both surgically treated isolated ACL injuries and MLKIs.

ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION TIMING

Arthrofibrosis of the knee joint is caused by excessive scar tissue formation, resulting
in pain and limited potential for the patient to regain the terminal 5 of extension

      effect on the risk of developing postoperative arthrofibrosis. A study performed in
      1991 found that open ACLR performed within a week of acute ACL injury resulted in
      an increased rate of postoperative stiffness compared with ACLR performed at least
      3 weeks from the time of acute ACL injury.14 In the same study, delayed surgery and
      accelerated rehabilitation (uncommon at the time) resulted in an earlier return of strength
      and a significantly lower incidence of arthrofibrosis. However, delayed ACLR has been
      associated with an increased risk of quadriceps atrophy, which may prolong postoper-
      ative rehabilitation and may negatively influence postoperative knee function.15
         With the advancement of arthroscopic knee surgery as the gold standard for the
      surgical treatment of ACL injury, the prevalence of arthrofibrosis and postoperative
      stiffness showed a diminishing tendency in patients undergoing ACLR, most likely
      due to early rehabilitation programs and improved surgical techniques.6 More recent
      studies failed to demonstrate increased rates of postoperative stiffness, arthrofibrosis,
      and ROM deficits with a variety of cutoff thresholds between early and delayed ACLR
      (<2 weeks, <3 weeks, <10 weeks and beyond).16 One RCT found that early (<8 days
      from injury to surgery) ACLR resulted in no ROM deficit at the 6-month or 24-month
      follow-up compared with delayed (6–10 weeks from injury to surgery) ACLR.1,17
      Additionally, early (<8 days from injury to surgery) surgery resulted in superior isoki-
      netic knee flexion strength at the 24-month follow-up compared with delayed (6–
      10 weeks from injury to surgery) treatment.17 Furthermore, a case series of early
      patellar tendon ACLRs (n 5 25) performed 9 days or lesser from injury to surgery
      did not identify any patients with a postoperative knee extension deficit greater than
      3 and knee flexion deficit greater than 5 compared with the contralateral knee at
      the final follow-up.18 Authors of the referenced studies highlight the prominent role
      of modern arthroscopic techniques and accelerated rehabilitation protocols to facili-
      tate early restoration of knee ROM during the postoperative period.17,18 In contrast,
      one recent retrospective study of 29,888 patients found that a 6 week or longer delay
      of ACLR reduces the 2-year likelihood of surgical treatment of arthrofibrosis by 65% in
      patients aged younger than 40 years.19 Although the timing of ACL surgery may affect
      the likelihood of postoperative arthrofibrosis, existing evidence suggests that early
      surgery combined with accelerated rehabilitation can lead to earlier return of strength
      and an infrequent incidence of arthrofibrosis. Conversely, delayed surgery may in-
      crease the risk of quadriceps atrophy and negatively influence postoperative knee
      function, especially problematic for high-level athletes who aim for rapid return to
      preinjury activity levels.


      COMPARISON OF CLINICAL OUTCOMES AFTER EARLY AND DELAYED ANTERIOR
      CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION

      During the years, surgical timing was determined as an influential factor on clinical out-
      comes after ACLR. Several studies compared the effects of early and delayed ACLR
      on the risk of graft failure and revision surgery. Economic and decision analysis using
      registry-based patient data from the Knee Anterior Cruciate Ligament Nonsurgical
      versus Surgical Treatment trial and Multicenter Orthopedic Outcomes Network cohort
      determined that early isolated ACLR results in less sick-leave days (on average
        31.6 days) and superior gains in Quality Adjusted Life Years compared with rehabil-
      itation with optional delayed ACLR. However, findings are conflicting regarding the as-
      sociation between ACLR timing and the risk of revision ACLR. One study of 11,867
      patients reported an increased risk of revision ACLR with delayed ACLR (performed
      at least 6 months after injury) compared with early ACLR (performed within 2 months

COMPARISON OF FUNCTIONAL OUTCOMES AFTER EARLY AND DELAYED ANTERIOR
CRUCIATE LIGAMENT RECONSTRUCTION

Another major controversy in ACL surgery is whether early or delayed ACLR leads to
superior objective and subjective outcomes for patients. Several studies report com-
parable clinical and outcomes superior knee stability because of both early and
delayed ACLR.24,25 One systematic review found similar tibiofemoral laxity, assessed
with the KT-1000 arthrometer, Lachman test, and the pivot shift test, in patients who
underwent early ACLR (performed within 1 month of injury) versus those who under-
went delayed ACLR (performed >8 weeks after injury).26 No significant differences
in postoperative knee ROM were found between the 2 groups.26 Additionally, one
recent study showed comparable patient-reported outcomes, with significant im-
provements in all subscales of the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score
(KOOS) and favorable return rate to preinjury Tegner activity level after both early
and delayed ACLR.17 Notably, a high proportion of patients in both the early and
delayed ACLR groups were able to return to Tegner activity level 6 or higher, suggest-
ing surgical timing may have a limited influence on the rate of return to sport.17 Further-
more, objective International Knee Documentation Committee scores were shown to
be similar among patient groups, with the majority of (82% vs 71%, respectively) of
patients having grade AB pivot shift at the 12-month postoperative follow-up, indica-
tive of restored knee laxity because of both early and delayed ACLR.17
   Further research showed that patients with early, hamstring tendon ACLR achieve
superior outcomes in terms of postoperative isokinetic knee flexion strength after
2 years compared with patients who underwent delayed ACLR.27 Specifically, patients
with early surgery achieved significantly greater improvement in flexor strength at 180
(8.1% improvement) and 240 (9.4% improvement) per second, without significant
improvement in extensor strength.27 In the same study, early ACLR was associated
with fewer sick-leave days and decreased socioeconomic costs compared with
delayed ACLR.27 Consequently, while both early and delayed surgery seem to yield
good to excellent functional outcomes, a combination of functional outcomes should
be assessed to determine the optimal timing of isolated ACLR.

of Secondary Intra-articular Injury

incidence of secondary intra-articular injury remains a topic of debate. Delayed sur-
gery was proposed to lead to meniscal8 and chondral7 damage secondary to knee
instability because of prolonged ACL deficiency.28

      AND CONCURRENT SURGICAL INTERVENTIONS

      Injury to the ACL is frequently accompanied by concomitant injuries and adequate
      treatment consists of addressing concurrent pathologic condition with concurrent
      surgical interventions. However, the interplay between additional surgical interven-
      tions concurrent with ACLR and surgical timing remains to be clarified. Patients with

study compared postoperative outcomes among a cohort of patients with early
(<8 weeks from injury to surgery) combined ACLR and anterolateral ligament (ALL)
reconstruction and a cohort with delayed (>8 weeks from injury to surgery) combined
ACLR and ALL reconstruction, with no differences in objective knee stability, subjec-
tive knee function, and graft failure rates (2.9% and 2.1%, respectively).40 Further-
more, patients with ACL injury often present with concomitant injury to the medial
collateral ligament (MCL).4,41 Although the choice between surgical or nonoperative
treatment of MCL injuries concomitant to ACLR remains a controversial topic, it was
recently reported that as few as 10% of patients nonoperatively treated for MCL injury
concurrent with ACLR return to preinjury activity level.42 Due to the detrimental effect
of persistent valgus laxity on the integrity of intra-articular soft-tissue, prolonged reha-
bilitation with incomplete healing and stress on the ACL graft, early combined ACLR
and MCL reconstruction is increasingly favored.43 Consequently, patients with antero-
lateral and anteromedial instability in the setting of surgically treated ACL injury may
benefit from early ACLR with concurrent lateral extra-articular tenodesis and MCL
reconstruction. Repair of treatable meniscus pathologic condition in conjunction
with ACLR is also considered advantageous in patients with ACL injury. It was reported
that 77.6% of meniscus injuries were repaired concomitant to early (<6 months from
injury to surgery) ACLR, whereas only 46.7% of meniscus injuries were repaired with
delayed (>6 months from injury to surgery) ACLR. Additionally, meniscus repair per-
formed in the setting of early (<48 hours from injury) ACLR resulted in lower rates of
extension deficit between 3 and 5 at the 12-month postoperative follow-up
compared with delayed (performed in the inflammation-free period) ACLR and
meniscus repair (3.7% vs 22.2%, respectively).11 Therefore, early surgical timing for
ACLR may be preferred in highly active patients with concurrent repairable meniscus
injury to prevent the incidence of downstream chondral wear and posttraumatic OA.

SUMMARY

In light of the current evidence, an improved understanding of surgical timing is war-
ranted to optimize patient outcomes with ACLR in the setting of isolated ACL and
MLKIs. Although interpretation of the existing data is hampered by inconsistent defi-
nitions of surgical timing, early ACLR performed within weeks of injury may result in
equivalent to superior clinical and functional outcomes. Importantly, early ACLR
seems to be beneficial for decreasing the incidence of medial meniscus and chondral
injury by avoiding prolonged knee instability, with excellent clinical and functional out-
comes and no marked increase in the risk of postoperative arthrofibrosis compared
with delayed surgery. Future studies are required to clarify the cutoff between early
and delayed surgeries to determine the influence of concurrent surgical procedures
on optimal surgical timing and to explore the role of surgical timing in the treatment
of patients with MLKIs.

  Delayed ACLR may increase the incidence of secondary intraarticular injuries and quadriceps

  Inconsistent definitions of early and delayed ACLR may lead to ambiguity and hinder

17	Abstract
18	Introduction Many professional football players sustain at least one severe injury over the course of their career. Because
19	detailed epidemiological data on different severe injuries in professional football have been missing so far, this study describes
20	the frequency and return-to-competition (RTC) periods of different types of severe football injuries.
21	Material and methods This epidemiological investigation is a prospective standardised injury analysis based on national
22	media longitudinal registration. Injuries were classified according to the consensus statement by Fuller et al. (2006). The
23	analysis includes injuries sustained by players of the first German football league during the seasons 2014–2015 to 2017–
24	2018. Level of evidence: II.
25	Results Overall, 660 severe injuries were registered during the four seasons (mean 165 per season; 9.2 per season per team;
26	incidence in 1000 h: 0.77). The body region most frequently affected by severe injury was the knee (30.0%; 49.5 injuries per
27	season/SD 13.2) followed by the thigh (26.4%; 43.5 injuries/SD 4.2) and the ankle (16.7%; 27.5 injuries/SD 5.0). The distri-
28	bution of injuries over the course of a season showed a trend for ACL ruptures to mainly occur at the beginning of a season
29	(45.8%), overuse syndromes such as achillodynia (40.9%) and irritation of the knee (44.4%) during the winter months and
30	severe muscle and ankle injuries at the end of a season. ACL ruptures showed the longest RTC durations (median 222 days).
31	Conclusion This study presents detailed epidemiological data on severe injuries in professional football. The body region
32	most frequently affected by severe injuries was the knee. Several types of severe injuries showed a seasonal injury pattern.
33	The appropriate timing of RTC after an injury is one of the most important and complex decisions to be made. This study
34	provides information on the typical time loss due to specific severe football injuries, which may serve as a guideline.

    ARTHROSCOPY AND SPORTS MEDICINE



Timing return‑to‑competition: a prospective registration of 45
different types of severe injuries in Germany’s highest football league
Werner Krutsch1,2 · Clemens Memmel3 · Volker Alt1 · Volker Krutsch4 · Tobias Tröß5 · Karen aus der Fünten5 ·
Tim Meyer5

Received: 17 December 2020 / Accepted: 2 March 2021
© The Author(s) 2021


Abstract
Introduction Many professional football players sustain at least one severe injury over the course of their career. Because
detailed epidemiological data on different severe injuries in professional football have been missing so far, this study describes
the frequency and return-to-competition (RTC) periods of different types of severe football injuries.
Material and methods This epidemiological investigation is a prospective standardised injury analysis based on national
media longitudinal registration. Injuries were classified according to the consensus statement by Fuller et al. (2006). The
analysis includes injuries sustained by players of the first German football league during the seasons 2014–2015 to 2017–
2018. Level of evidence: II.
Results Overall, 660 severe injuries were registered during the four seasons (mean 165 per season; 9.2 per season per team;
incidence in 1000 h: 0.77). The body region most frequently affected by severe injury was the knee (30.0%; 49.5 injuries per
season/SD 13.2) followed by the thigh (26.4%; 43.5 injuries/SD 4.2) and the ankle (16.7%; 27.5 injuries/SD 5.0). The distri-
bution of injuries over the course of a season showed a trend for ACL ruptures to mainly occur at the beginning of a season
(45.8%), overuse syndromes such as achillodynia (40.9%) and irritation of the knee (44.4%) during the winter months and
severe muscle and ankle injuries at the end of a season. ACL ruptures showed the longest RTC durations (median 222 days).
Conclusion This study presents detailed epidemiological data on severe injuries in professional football. The body region
most frequently affected by severe injuries was the knee. Several types of severe injuries showed a seasonal injury pattern.
The appropriate timing of RTC after an injury is one of the most important and complex decisions to be made. This study
provides information on the typical time loss due to specific severe football injuries, which may serve as a guideline.

In 53 studies (79%), fatigue produced changes linked to higher ACL injury risk, such as less knee flexion, more knee abduction, or more anterior tibial translation.",
30	 "screeningLimitations": "The Methods report 60 articles included for extraction while the Results and abstract report 67, so the final sample is unclear. 35	  "doi": "10.3390/biomechanics5010011",
36	  "abstract": "Structured review of lower-limb neuromuscular fatigue as an ACL injury risk factor, covering 67 studies and 1440 healthy young adults. Studies were included if they compared fatigued and non-fatigued states and measured at least one biomechanical variable linked to ACL injury.",
37	  "tldr": "Localised leg-muscle fatigue changed biomechanics in a way linked to ACL injury risk in most studies, so it looks like one modifiable risk factor among several. Fatigue protocols and measures vary so much that there is no consensus on how to test it.",
38	  "methods": "Structured Medline search run on 23 June 2023, with two-stage screening and data extraction. Included studies used healthy participants aged 18 to 35 and compared fatigued with non-fatigued states on at least one lower-limb biomechanical variable. Outcomes were coded as kinematic, kinetic, neuromuscular or proprioceptive and classed as increasing or decreasing ACL risk. No pooled meta-analysis was run.",
39	  "findings": "Of 67 studies, 53 (79%) reported post-fatigue changes indicating higher ACL injury risk, such as reduced knee flexion, increased knee abduction or internal rotation, and increased anterior tibial translation. Fatigue protocols and end-points were highly variable, including volitional failure, RPE thresholds and fixed-time or cycle criteria. Only one study objectively measured neuromuscular fatigue, using EMG mean power frequency.",
40	  "limitations": "Methods report 60 articles for extraction while Results report 67, so the sample size is unclear. There is no pooled estimate or formal risk-of-bias rating, most protocols did not measure fatigue objectively, and the included participants were healthy young adults, many of them physically active rather than athletes.",
41	  "practicalImplications": "Assessing movement in a fatigued state, and training controlled landing and cutting while tired, may be useful within ACL injury-risk programmes. The authors also suggest neuromuscular endurance work, which the included studies did not test.",
42	  "athleteDev": "Supports checking landing and cutting quality after sport-specific fatigue as part of ACL injury-risk work. The fatigue protocols are not standardised, so no single protocol should be treated as validated for an individual athlete.",
43	  "rtp": "Relevant to return-to-sport testing because the authors suggest assessing movement in a fatigued state, but the review excluded participants after ACL reconstruction and so does not show outcomes after surgery or clearance criteria."

73	                           factors that would allow clinicians, rehabilitation specialists, and researchers to develop
74	                           and apply effective injury risk reducing interventions. Although there still remains debate
75	                           around the association of biomechanical factors and the risk of ACL injury [8], of the
76	                           most cited and investigated modifiable biomechanical risk factors are those related to an
77	                           individual’s lower extremity kinematics and kinetics. Boden et al. (2007) [9] analyzed
78	                           videos of professional basketball players performing decelerations and landing maneuvers
79	                           to quantify knee joint kinematics and compared them between individuals who suffered an
80	                           ACL injury and healthy controls. They found that initiating decelerations and landings with
81	                           the heel increased the risk of ACL injury as the impact could not be adequately absorbed
82	                           throughout the kinetic chain. Prospective research, such as that conducted by Hewett et al.
83	                           (2005) [10], showed that an increased knee valgus angle and abduction moment during
84	                           jump landings at baseline testing increased an athlete’s risk of ACL injury throughout their
85	                           competitive season. Krosshaug et al. (2016) [11] also identified medial knee displacement
86	                           as a risk factor in individuals who had previously experienced an ACL injury. Although
87	                           Leppanen et al. (2017) [12] did not identify knee valgus as a risk factor for ACL injury, they
88	                           did identify that increases in vertical ground forces increased injury risk.
89	                                 Further to this, strain on the ACL caused by anterior translation has been shown to be
90	                           greater than the strain caused by isolated knee valgus forces or internal rotation moments.
91	                           For example, 100 N of anterior translation resulted in 3.7% ACL strain, while 200 N of valgus
92	                           and 10 Nm of internal rotation produced only 2.5% and 2.0% ACL strain, respectively [13].
93	                           However, combinations of anterior translation, valgus, internal rotation, and near end-
94	                           range extension have also been implicated as a common ACL injury mechanism [14].
95	                                 There appears to be a relative consensus that some patterns of lower extremity joint
96	                           kinematics and kinetics have a role in inducing ACL injuries. A potential modulator
97	                           of this is neuromuscular fatigue that occurs to the musculature of the lower extremity.
98	                           Neuromuscular fatigue, defined as a change in the force generating capacity of the muscle
99	                           along with alterations in the firing patterns at the neuromuscular junction [15], may result
100	                           in altered motor unit recruitment (i.e., fatigue affects both the magnitude and timing of
101	                           muscle force production), which in turn may lead to changes in the kinematics at the
102	                           affected joint(s). It is the altered kinematics that are suggested to be responsible for an
103	                           increase in ACL injury risk.
104	                                 In the most general sense, neuromuscular fatigue can be referred to as a change in
105	                           the force-generating capacity of the muscle along with alterations in the firing patterns at
106	                           the neuromuscular junction and incorporates both central and peripheral processes [15].
107	                           However, it has been argued that this definition alone does not fully encapsulate the range of
108	                           fatiguing processes and the effect these have on all types of performance [16]. Alternatively,
109	                           Enoka and Duchateau (2016) [16] proposed a taxonomy of fatigue that addresses the two
110	                           main attributes of fatigue: (i) performance fatigability and (ii) perceived fatigability. In the
111	                           simplest form, however, performance fatigability includes those processes and outcomes
112	                           that result in a decline in objective measures of fatigue such as contractile function and
113	                           muscle activation. Perceived fatigability, however, relates to the sensations of fatigue
114	                           that affect performance and includes both homeostasis and the psychological state of the
115	                           individual. While it is important to understand this process, these taxonomies [16,17] are
116	                           still governed by central and peripheral processes of fatigue.
117	                                 While the Enoka and Duchateau provides a mechanism to categorize different types
118	                           of fatigue, this framework was further updated by Behrens et al. (2023) [17] to parse out the

127	                           the performance of the central nervous system. Finally, a major strength of the updated
128	                           framework is the acknowledgment that the measurement of state fatigue should include
129	                           objective measures and that the onset and measurement of motor and cognitive fatigue can
130	                           be affected by perceived fatigue.

134	                           junction (NMJ). In their review, Taylor et al. (2016) [18] categorized central fatigue primarily
135	                           as the decreased stimulatory output of motor neurons caused by either a decrease in their

137	                           Fuglvand’s [15] description of firing-rate adaptation, where over time and with a constant
138	                           excitatory drive, the neural inhibition of muscle activity rises exponentially to limit force
139	                           production before the signal reaches the muscle. These aspects of central fatigue could be
140	                           categorized as performance fatigability [16] or perceived motor and cognitive fatigue [17].
141	                                Cognitive or mental fatigue is another type of centralized fatigue and was defined
142	                           by Marcora et al. (2009) [19] as “a psychobiological state caused by prolonged exposure
143	                           to a cognitively demanding task where individuals may report feelings of tiredness or
144	                           lack of energy”; or, according to the previously defined taxonomy, aspects of perceived
145	                           fatigability. To induce this type of fatigue, researchers have typically asked participants
146	                           to complete a difficult cognitive task; however, this type of fatigue is difficult to measure
147	                           and quantify. Cutsem et al. (2017) [20] performed a systematic review that included
148	                           11 studies describing and attempting to quantify the effect of mental and/or cognitive

150	                           consistent decrease in endurance performance, accompanied by an increase in the athletes’

152	                           markers of endurance fatigue (e.g., increased heart rate, increased lactate concentration) or
153	                           changes in strength and power. This suggests that psychological or cognitive fatigue may
154	                           be different, and elicit different responses, compared to neuromuscular fatigue.

158	                           and distal to the NMJ [15]. This often involves the force-generating capabilities and
159	                           intrinsic fatiguability of motor units (MUs) within a muscle and can be categorized as
160	                           performance fatigability [16,17]. Burke et al. (1973) [21] described this as a decrease in force
161	                           capacity within a muscle after repetitive stimulation. Potvin and Fuglevand (2017) [15] also

                           objective measures and that the onset and measurement of motor and cognitive fatigue can
                           be affected by perceived fatigue.

                           1.1. Central Fatigue
                                Central fatigue refers to fatigue-related processes proximal to and at the neuromuscular
                           junction (NMJ). In their review, Taylor et al. (2016) [18] categorized central fatigue primarily
                           as the decreased stimulatory output of motor neurons caused by either a decrease in their
                           excitatory output or an increase in their inhibitory output. This is similar to Potvin and
                           Fuglvand’s [15] description of firing-rate adaptation, where over time and with a constant
                           excitatory drive, the neural inhibition of muscle activity rises exponentially to limit force
                           production before the signal reaches the muscle. These aspects of central fatigue could be
                           categorized as performance fatigability [16] or perceived motor and cognitive fatigue [17].
                                Cognitive or mental fatigue is another type of centralized fatigue and was defined
                           by Marcora et al. (2009) [19] as “a psychobiological state caused by prolonged exposure
                           to a cognitively demanding task where individuals may report feelings of tiredness or
                           lack of energy”; or, according to the previously defined taxonomy, aspects of perceived
                           fatigability. To induce this type of fatigue, researchers have typically asked participants
                           to complete a difficult cognitive task; however, this type of fatigue is difficult to measure
                           and quantify. Cutsem et al. (2017) [20] performed a systematic review that included
                           11 studies describing and attempting to quantify the effect of mental and/or cognitive
                           fatigue on aerobic performance. Overall, they reported that cognitive fatigue led to a
                           consistent decrease in endurance performance, accompanied by an increase in the athletes’
                           rate of perceived exertion. However, this was not accompanied by any physiological
                           markers of endurance fatigue (e.g., increased heart rate, increased lactate concentration) or
                           changes in strength and power. This suggests that psychological or cognitive fatigue may
                           be different, and elicit different responses, compared to neuromuscular fatigue.

                           1.2. Peripheral Fatigue
                                 Peripheral [16], or motor performance [17], fatigue primarily refers to fatigue at
                           and distal to the NMJ [15]. This often involves the force-generating capabilities and
                           intrinsic fatiguability of motor units (MUs) within a muscle and can be categorized as
                           performance fatigability [16,17]. Burke et al. (1973) [21] described this as a decrease in force
                           capacity within a muscle after repetitive stimulation. Potvin and Fuglevand (2017) [15] also
                           examined this principle in their muscle fatigue model. This model simulates peripheral
                           fatigue following sustained contractions with marked decreases in contractile speed where
                           decreases were greatest in the stronger, most fatigable MUs. It is this type of localized
                           fatigue that we hypothesize primarily contributes to ACL injuries.
                                 Despite the current understanding of the types and process of fatigue, fatigue as
                           an injury risk factor or fatigue as an injury mechanism has remained contentious in the
                           literature for a variety of reasons. Therefore, the purposes of this review are (i) to present
                           the research and practical concepts of lower extremity neuromuscular fatigue; and (ii) to
                           review the literature related to neuromuscular fatigue as an ACL injury risk factor and
                           mechanism.
 Biomechanics 2025, 5, 11                                                                                                                          4 of 21



                                          2. A Review: Fatigue and ACL Injuries
                                          Search and Analysis Methods
                                                A structured approach to the literature search was taken to ensure that a thorough,
                                          broad, and representative sample of literature was collected and reviewed. The Medline
                                          database was searched on 23 June 2023, using a structured search strategy that included
                                          terms such as “anterior cruciate ligament injury” and “knee injuries” combined with terms
                                          such as “injury” and “fatigue”. Details of the full search strategy can be found in the
                                          Supplemental Materials. Initially, 577 articles were included (567 from the initial search
                                          and 10 after searching reference lists) with 30 duplicates removed (Figure 1). Articles were
                                          included if (1) they involved young healthy participants (18–35); (2) made a comparison
                                          between non-fatigued and fatigued states; (3) measured at least one lower extremity
                                          biomechanical variable associated with ACL injury risk; and ((4) was published within the

                                          (2) studied participants post-ACLR; and/or (3) specifically studied runners with a focus on
                                          running biomechanics. Systematic reviews were also excluded. After screening, a total of
                                          60 articles were included for data extraction.
